title.narrative: Integrated Natural Resources Management for Improved Ecosystem Conservation and Biodiversity Preservation

description.narrative: E.1 Knowledge Management and Communication129. This Project Document adopts the GEF definitions for ‘knowledge’ and ‘knowledge management (KM) [16]. Knowledge management involves a strategic and multidisciplinary approach. This includes a series of activities that address key issues of the project, with a strong emphasis on integrating gender perspectives to address gaps and drive change. The project’s KM strategy is twofold: the Uzbekistan Child Project dimension which focuses on leveraging project experience to support learning and policy updates among project target audiences. This is backed up by a dedicated budget for Knowledge Management in Component 5. For more on the Uzbekistan KM aspects, see the Rationale and Annex E under Component 5.130. The second dimension is the linkage with the CAWLN coordination project, which will establish the framework for knowledge management across the region and facilitate the exchange of best practices and lessons learned among the five countries. The six CAWLN Child Projects (CPs) will contribute knowledge products in best practices, and lessons learned to the Coordination child project, which will serve as the primary hub for knowledge-sharing across all projects. This project will ensure that its M&E processes feed into this platform, and relevant outputs (e.g. case studies, reports) will be shared with IW:LEARN and other GEF platforms. The Coordination child project, on the other hand, will take the lead in consolidating and disseminating knowledge across all country projects, acting as the main interface with IW:LEARN and organizing regional knowledge-sharing events and capacity-building activities. It will also maintain the central platform for coordinating inputs and results from all projects.131. Aligned with the CAWLN Program KM Strategy, the Uzbekistan Child Project KM strategy will maximize the Program impact by: · Following the systematically sharing knowledge assets generated with the intended beneficiaries and audiences in vertical and horizontal ways;· Supporting the science-policy interface (SPI) and influencing decision-making through data and information sharing, capacity building, and regional stakeholder engagement; · Promoting incremental innovation within GEF programmatic approaches and enriching the knowledge base of GEF Implementing and Executing Agencies. 132. The project KM approach will focus on three pillars: Collection, Analysis, and Dissemination of knowledge related to project activities, best practices, and lessons learned. The key components of the KM approach are: Budget (Described in Annex D - Budget and Workplan): Data Collection and Analysis Tools (Means of Verification): $264.000 Training and Capacity Building activities (throughout the components): $208.200 Knowledge Sharing and Dissemination Platforms and Events: $80.000 Key Deliverables (Described in Annex C - Results Framework): Development of a KM Framework that outlines processes for knowledge capture, storage, and sharing Creation of a centralized Knowledge Repository accessible to all stakeholders (CAWLN Knowledge Sharing Platform and IW:LEARN Platform) Regular Knowledge Sharing and Dissemination Workshops and Seminars Monitoring of GESI and GEB (during PMU meetings) Publication of case studies and best practice reports based on project experiences Implementation of an online platform for collaboration and sharing among project stakeholders Timeline (Described in Annex D - Budget and Workplan): Month 1-4: Develop KM strategic document and set up Knowledge Repository Quarterly (Years 1, 2 and 3): Conduct Workshops and Seminars on Project Outcomes and Best Practices Specific timepoints (Years 1, 2 and 3): Conduct Workshops and training sessions for target audiences Quarterly (Years 2 and 3): Organize quarterly workshops (during PMU meetings) and synthesize lessons learned into reports Quarterly (Years 2 and 3): Evaluate KM effectiveness and update strategies based on stakeholder feedback 133. In terms of communication, the project will ensure the effective dissemination of knowledge and best practices which will be supported by the development of a gender-sensitive communication strategy. The communication strategy will focus on sharing and publicizing project results to partners, stakeholders and general society. The objective is to enlarge project visibility, results and new initiatives implemented in the field, seeking to promote project credibility, transparency and legitimacy. 134. The project communication strategy will focus on both the project implementation itself by facilitating effective communication within the project team and with the project main partners, and publicizing project actions and results to the broader public by sharing its contributions, advancements, lessons learned and good practices to encourage replication and scaling up. 135. During the execution of capacity-building and awareness-raising activities, the project will consider the distribution of communication materials (flyers, cards, etc.) related to the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) policies developed by FAO. All of this is framed within the Zero-Tolerance Policy of the United Nations System Toward Gender-Based Abuse and Violence, including sexual harassment, abuse, and exploitation. E.2 Socio-economic Benefits and Decent Rural Employment [17] 136. The proposed project aims to deliver significant socio-economic benefits at both the national and local levels in Uzbekistan. At the national level, the project will enhance environmental sustainability by promoting the harmonious integration of water and land management practices, which will further support the country's commitment to biodiversity conservation and climate resilience. By implementing these sustainable practices, the project will address key environmental challenges, such as land degradation and reduced agrobiodiversity, ultimately contributing to the global objectives of combating climate change and preserving critical ecosystem services. 137. Moreover, the project will have tangible socio-economic impacts at the local level, particularly for rural communities where agricultural productivity and livelihoods are threatened by unsustainable practices and environmental degradation. By supporting investments in sustainable land and water management and strengthening community-based resource management, the project will create job opportunities and generate income for local populations. Additionally, promoting biodiversity-friendly practices and enhancing resilience in agricultural systems will ensure food security and economic stability for rural households. 138. Social benefits include the empowerment of local communities through the revitalization of traditional practices and cultural heritage. Women’s unique knowledge of agrobiodiversity and CWR will be recognized in ways that enhance their social standing in communities. Inclusive and participatory approaches will foster equitable distribution of the benefits derived from sustainable resource management, promoting social cohesion. Resilience and food security will be enhanced for vulnerable smallholders. 139. Furthermore, in project areas, the project will actively promote decent work and productive employment in rural areas, aligning with international labor principles. Through capacity-building activities, training programs, and the dissemination of best practices, the project will empower local communities to engage in sustainable agriculture and natural resource management practices, enhancing their livelihoods and overall well-being. This will be achieved through a package including support for farmers to identify market opportunities while facilitating a fair and sustainable agrobiodiversity value chain. Project actions align with Pillar 1 of FAO’s Decent Work Agenda [18], supporting employment creation and enterprise development. By fostering inclusive and participatory approaches, the project will ensure equitable distribution of the benefits derived from sustainable resource management, promoting social cohesion and economic development across Uzbekistan's rural landscape. To enable a transformative shift towards resilience and sustainability in the management of natural resources, especially the harmonious integration of water and land management practices, in order to improve biodiversity conservation and environmental sustainability of food systems in Uzbekistan
